content: Plum pox, also referred to as sharka, is the most destructive viral disease affecting stone fruits within the genus Prunus. This disease is caused by the plum pox virus (PPV), which exists in different strains capable of infecting a variety of stone fruit species, including peaches, apricots, plums, nectarines, almonds, and both sweet and tart cherries. Additionally, wild and ornamental species of Prunus can also be infected by certain strains of the virus. The virus is primarily transmitted by aphids and through the movement of infected plant material to new locations. While plum pox does not pose any health risks to consumers, it significantly impacts the marketability of stone fruits by causing deformities and increased acidity. The only effective method to manage the disease is the removal and destruction of all infected trees, which can result in substantial economic losses. Although a genetically modified plum resistant to the plum pox virus has been developed, it is not yet commercially available. The plum pox virus is a linear, single-stranded RNA virus. There are four recognized strains of the virus: PPV-D, PPV-M, PPV-EA, and PPV-C. Among these, PPV-M is particularly aggressive in peaches, is transmitted more efficiently by aphids, and spreads more rapidly within orchards. Unlike other strains, PPV-M has been reported to be transmitted through seeds, while the other strains are not known to spread via this route. Both PPV-M and PPV-D infect peaches, plums, and apricots. PPV-C, on the other hand, naturally infects sweet and tart cherries and is the only strain known to do so, although it has been shown to infect other Prunus species under experimental conditions. Several species of aphids are capable of transmitting the plum pox virus within orchards and over short distances, typically up to 200–300 meters, to nearby trees. Unlike persistent viruses such as the barley yellow dwarf virus, PPV is non-persistent in aphids and is transmitted mechanically via their mouthparts during feeding. Long-distance spread of the virus generally occurs through the movement of infected nursery stock or propagative materials. Once a tree is infected, the virus becomes systemic, spreading throughout the cytoplasm of cells in all parts of the plant. Infected trees experience a significant reduction in fruit production, and the fruits that are produced are often misshapen and blemished. Furthermore, the presence of plum pox can exacerbate the effects of other endemic viruses infecting Prunus species, such as prune dwarf virus, Prunus necrotic ringspot virus, and apple chlorotic leaf spot virus, leading to even greater economic losses. In peaches, infected trees may display color-breaking symptoms in their blossoms, characterized by darker pink stripes on the flower petals. This symptom can be useful for early-season surveys. Symptoms may also appear on young leaves in the spring or on developing fruit. However, some trees may not exhibit any visible symptoms on their leaves or fruit. Infections in Prunus species are not always associated with the characteristic ring symptoms on leaves. Instead, some cultivars may show yellowing line patterns, blotches, or necrotic ring symptoms on expanded leaves. Leaf distortion has also been observed. Infected fruits may develop yellow or brown rings or blotches, and some plums and apricots may become severely deformed and bumpy. The seeds of many infected apricots and some plums may also display ring symptoms. Beyond Prunus species, at least nine other plant families have been artificially infected with one or more strains of the plum pox virus, and in some cases, natural infections have been observed in the field. The ability of the virus to persist in non-Prunus species complicates efforts to manage the disease. There is currently no cure or treatment for plum pox once a tree is infected. The only option is to destroy infected trees. Once the disease becomes established, control and prevention strategies include conducting field surveys, using certified nursery materials, controlling aphid populations, and removing infected trees from nurseries and orchards. While some sources of resistance to the virus exist within Prunus species, they are uncommon. A team of scientists from the United States and France has successfully developed a genetically engineered plum, known as C5, that is resistant to the plum pox virus. This resistance is achieved through the expression of the virus's coat protein, which triggers a defense mechanism called post-transcriptional gene silencing (PTGS), similar to RNA interference (RNAi). The resistance trait can be passed on to other plum trees through hybridization, providing a valuable resource for future breeding programs. However, similar success has not yet been achieved in genetically modifying other Prunus species, although research efforts are ongoing. In the fall of 1999, the PPV-D strain of plum pox was detected in an orchard in Adams County, Pennsylvania, marking the first occurrence of the disease in North America. The affected areas in Pennsylvania were placed under quarantine to prevent further spread, and infected trees were destroyed. Subsequent surveys in 2000 revealed additional cases in Nova Scotia and Southern Ontario, particularly in the Niagara Region. In response, the Canadian Food Inspection Agency established quarantine zones throughout Southern Ontario to contain the virus. Despite extensive surveys, the virus has not been detected in other areas of Canada with susceptible trees. The Canadian plum pox eradication initiative has involved testing a large number of samples for the virus using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) technology. Over the past five years, the University of Guelph's Laboratory Services Division has conducted more than 2,000,000 tests in support of this initiative.
